title: Color and Color Vision
lead: The retina senses light with rods and three types of cones, and the hues we perceive come from the ways light stimulates the three types of cones. The simplified theory of color vision builds on this. Wavelengths set both the true color of an object and the color of a light source, and the eye and brain keep the colors of objects constant under different lights.
objectives: Explain the simple theory of color vision.
Outline the coloring properties of light sources.
Describe the retinex theory of color vision.
summary_html:
• The eye has four types of light receptors—rods and three types of color-sensitive cones.
  • The rods are good for night vision, peripheral vision, and motion changes, while the cones are responsible for central vision and color.
  • We perceive many hues, from light having mixtures of wavelengths.
  • A simplified theory of color vision states that there are three primary colors, which correspond to the three types of cones, and that various combinations of the primary colors produce all the hues.
  • The true color of an object is related to its relative absorption of various wavelengths of light. The color of a light source is related to the wavelengths it produces.
  • Color constancy is the ability of the eye-brain system to discern the true color of an object illuminated by various light sources.
  • The retinex theory of color vision explains color constancy by postulating the existence of three retinexes or image systems, associated with the three types of cones that are compared to obtain sophisticated information.

figures.original_caption: The image shows the relative sensitivity of the three types of cones, which are named according to wavelengths of greatest sensitivity. Rods are about 1000 times more sensitive, and their curve peaks at about 500 nm. Evidence for the three types of cones comes from direct measurements in animal and human eyes and testing of people with color blindness.

Absorption characteristics determine the true color of an object. Here, three objects are illuminated by white light, and one by pure red light. White is the equal mixture of all visible wavelengths; black is the absence of light.

Emission spectra for various light sources are shown. Curve A is average sunlight at Earth’s surface, curve B is light from a fluorescent lamp, and curve C is the output of an incandescent light. The spike for a helium-neon laser (curve D) is due to its pure wavelength emission. The spikes in the fluorescent output are due to atomic spectra—a topic that will be explored later.

The importance of edges is shown. Although the grey strips are uniformly shaded, as indicated by the graph immediately below them, they do not appear uniform at all. Instead, they are perceived darker on the dark side and lighter on the light side of the edge, as shown in the bottom graph. This is due to nerve impulse processing in the eye.

exercises.prompt: A student sees a piece of paper sitting on a table. Which of the following would not result in the student observing the paper as yellow?

options: Yellow light shines on a black paper.
White light shines on a yellow paper.
Yellow light shines on a white paper.
Red and green lights shine on a white paper.
answer.hint: The paper can only send to the eye the light that falls on it and that it does not absorb.

exercises.prompt: A white light is projected onto a tablecloth. Using the light reflecting off the tablecloth, an observer determines that the color of the tablecloth is blue. (a) Using the wave model of light, explain how the observer is capable of making this judgment. (b) Describe how using the particle model of light limits our explanation of the observer’s judgment.

answer.solution: (a) In the wave model, white light is a mixture of waves of all visible wavelengths. The tablecloth absorbs most wavelengths and reflects mainly the short wavelengths near 450 nm. Those reflected waves stimulate the blue cones far more than the green and red cones, and the eye-brain system interprets that ratio of stimulations as blue. (b) A model that treats light only as a stream of particles gives no property that changes from one color to another. By itself it cannot say why the cloth absorbs some light and reflects some, or why the reflected light looks blue. Wavelength describes color naturally, and wavelength belongs to the wave model.

exercises.prompt: A pure red object on a black background seems to disappear when illuminated with pure green light. Explain why.

answer.solution: A pure red object reflects only red light and absorbs every other wavelength. Under pure green light it absorbs all the light that falls on it and reflects nothing, so it appears black. The black background also reflects nothing, so the object cannot be told from its background and seems to disappear.

exercises.prompt: What is color constancy, and what are its limitations?

answer.solution: Color constancy is the ability of the eye-brain system to perceive the true color of an object under different lighting, by comparing the object with its surroundings; a white tablecloth looks white in sunlight, fluorescent light, or candlelight. It has limits. It needs surroundings to compare with, so an object seen alone, or a whole scene lit by strongly colored light such as the pure red light of a laser or a single-color street lamp, is not corrected, and an object that reflects nothing of the light falling on it still appears black.

exercises.prompt: There are different types of color blindness related to the malfunction of different types of cones. Why would it be particularly useful to study those rare individuals who are color blind only in one eye or who have a different type of color blindness in each eye?

answer.solution: Such a person can compare, with the same brain, what each eye sees of the same scene. The normal eye gives a reference, so the person can describe how colors look to the color-blind eye, something a person color blind in both eyes can never report. Comparing two eyes with different types of color blindness shows directly what each type of cone contributes to the perception of hues.

exercises.prompt: Propose a way to study the function of the rods alone, given they can sense light about 1000 times dimmer than the cones.

answer.solution: Let the subject adapt to the dark and then show test images at a light level too dim to stimulate the cones but bright enough for the rods, less than about one thousandth of the level the cones need. Whatever the subject can then detect, such as shapes, grey levels, motion, or objects in the peripheral field, is detected by the rods alone, and the absence of color confirms that the cones are not responding.
